utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise one preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This submission relates to the Chamber's request of the 22nd of November that the Prosecution indicate by the 2nd of December which redactions it would seek to lift in response to the recent Appeals Chamber decision regarding adjudicated facts. As the Chamber will recall, the Prosecution in its 20 November motion, has -- has moved the Chamber to take judicial notice of reformulated impugned facts reformulated in a way which we believe conforms to the Appeals Chamber's decision. The exhibits that we will seek to lift some of the redactions from will depend in significant part on the Chamber's decision on this application. While we will begin and have begun the process of reviewing the evidence to be unredacted, the decision ultimately is dependant upon the Prosecution knowing what is the final set of adjudicated facts upon which we can rely. Something which in turn is dependant on the Chamber's decision. We have already begun the process and will aim to place ourselves in a position to respond quickly once this Chamber enters its decision on our motion for the reformulation of these facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your submission. Yes. Is the Prosecution ready to call its -- yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are ready to call the next witness but there are some residual matters relating to Mr. Brown, the tendering of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. We could deal with them right away. Let me just have a look. I think MFI numbers P2859 through 2863 are reports and statements and errata sheets which still need to be decided upon -- still need to be tendered. We will then hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour probably can't see Mr. Traldi to my right but he will be dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see him as a matter of fact. He was hidden behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I'll try to lean so don't have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if we do both then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is those five MFI numbers that are also associated exhibits to the statement which I'm prepared to address if the statement were to be admitted. But, first, I'd tender MFI P2859 through 2863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Defence? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can go one at a time if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just briefly mention them then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: P2859 is the Krajina report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Krajina report. Seems to be a problem with the microphone of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, this one doesn't work. We stand by all the objections we already raised previously. And we think that especially this Krajina report has a lot of wrong quotations and wrong references. I didn't have time to go through all of them, but -- and we are not going to show the Prosecution where those mistakes are. That's their job. We will probably bring the witness who would refute the work of Mr. Ewan Brown, and in that work, we will show all the flaws this report has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we will probably have more additional and -- not at this time. I showed a couple of them on Friday, but there are more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in the context of admission if you say: I'm not going to show the other ones, then it's impossible for the Prosecution to pay further attention to it, and the Chamber necessarily has rely on the ones you showed. If you think that the Chamber would go through every footnote and see whether possibly there could be a mistake with an underlying document which is not in evidence, then you are wrong. So, therefore, if you refrain from further explaining where the errors are, then we have to rely on what you've shown to us until now. We have to assess the importance of those errors, the type of errors. So it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you should turn to the Prosecution and ask them where the errors are in their witness's report. Not to ask Defence to show the Chamber where the mistakes are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I told you what the consequences are of this approach. I further -- Mr. Lukic, if we would follow you, we would never know because there would be no need to call any witnesses later to explain to us why Mr. Brown was wrong because then it would not be in evidence. So anything else in relation to 2859, the Krajina report?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about mistakes we showed, whether -- are they going to be part of this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the Chamber will always look at the evidence in its entirety. So if any mistake or error was demonstrated during the examination -- examination of the witness, then, of course, we'll take that into account in the evaluation of the report as part of the totality of the evidence. If we would admit it. Anything else, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, that's -- that's in addition to the written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- objections we had previously to this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, having heard the parties, admits into evidence P2859, the Krajina report. Next one, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the next two, P2860 and 2861, the two errata sheets to that report, probably raise the same issues and can be addressed together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There some of the errors were already addressed. They are, of course, they not be separate from the -- from the report itself. Mr. Lukic, anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems those errata sheets are not complete. We would object to them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are not going to tell us in what respect they are wrong. Therefore, the Chamber, having heard the parties and relying on the submissions made until now, admits into evidence P2860 and P2861. Next one, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: P2862, Mr. President, is the witness's Manjaca report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, apart from the objections already made, anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2862 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, P2863 is the witness's statement which we tendered 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We objected to this statement as well, since I think that statement is actually doing the Chamber's work. Analysing documents. Nothing in that statement is actually a statement. Just an analysis of documents that we consider is job of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Chamber will finally analyse and evaluate the -- the reports and the documents but considers that it is assisted by what the witness told us about it. P2863 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regarding the associated exhibits to Mr. Brown's statement, Your Honour, as I suggested last Monday, we've reduced the number to be tendered compared to the 92 ter motion by about 50 per cent. There are 19 remaining. Of those, nine were in our municipalities bar table motion and met with no objection in the Defence's response. Under those circumstances, I'd note your observation during cross-examination, Mr. President, that in the absence of an objection, whether the exhibits come in from the bar table or through the witness is not of primary importance and I'd suggest that it's most efficient to have these nine admitted now. I can just go through the 65 ter numbers for those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would do that. They are mainly the underlying documents to the -- at least to statement and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: All of these are associated exhibits to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So the nine that met with no objection in the bar table motion are 00678, 06802, 07042, 07152, 07154, 07159, 08392, 10791, and 22883B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the nine numbers for these documents range from?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P2905 up to and including P2913, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2905 through P2913 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And regarding the other ten, Mr. President, I'd suggest we might go one by one so that if there any question whether they are appropriate as associated, it can be addressed orally now. The first is 03324.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have those documents with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll delay that and we'll deal with that at a later stage. Mr. Traldi, I suggest that you make a short -- if you put all the numbers in one small document so that Madam Registrar can reserve numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic will then prepare for any response to be heard. Mr. Lukic, later this week. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Traldi. That's -- or is there any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Two other brief follow-up matters regarding Mr. Brown. First, in compliance with the Chamber's guidance, we may file a bar table motion regarding expert Brown related to specific areas challenged during cross-examination. It may be that for a number of issues we can reduce the number of exhibits in that motion by referring to exhibits already in evidence or tendered in other bar table motions. To focus the record, we will do so wherever possible. Additionally, Mr. Lukic inquired on cross-examination about the prosecution of the persons who killed Mr. Bender and Mr. Filipovic at Manjaca. I note that this has been raised with several witnesses now and we would invite the Defence to propose an agreed fact on this topic. Mr. Lukic also put to Mr. Brown that this prosecution was done on the basis of evidence gathered during the war. If the Defence provides evidence to support that proposition, we are open to agreeing on that point as well. That concludes my submission related to expert Brown. Begging the Chamber's indulgence, I would raise one other time-sensitive preliminary matter which is to request an additional two weeks for the reply to the Defence's response to the municipalities bar table motion. The Defence received approximately two months additional for their response and we would request two weeks additional for the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see ... Yes, we'll consider that and let you know as soon as possible, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then I'd just request to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Hasan, that is -- no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. I'd only request that he be given a Rule 90(E) caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, before we start hearing your evidence, I'd like to inform you about your rights. If any of the answers you would give on one of the questions would tend to incriminate yourself, then you may object to answer such question. We, however, the Chamber, could compel you to answer that question despite that objection; but if we would compel you to answer the question in this way, then that could not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against yourself for any offence, apart from the offence of giving false testimony. Has this been explained to you prior to coming to court, that you have this right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has. I have already appeared in this courtroom as a witness before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, we want to repeat it now so that you are fully aware of your position in this respect. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now there's another preliminary matter, Ms. Hasan, which is the following, that we have not yet received a response to the 92 ter motion, so if you want to proceed on the basis of 92 ter, we should first hear from the Defence. And if I'm not mistaken, there was -- in that request was also a 92 bis request, which may need an answer, but I also can imagine that the Defence would like to respond in writing. But today the Defence response to the 92 ter motion is due, Mr. Stojanovic. What is the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. We are prepared to cross-examine this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you do not object to him being examined in chief on the basis of 92 ter. Then leave is granted to hear the testimony of this witness under Rule 92 ter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning -- good morning, Witness. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, have you recently had the opportunity to review or -- to review in a language that you understand the interview you gave at the Belgrade field office on the 2nd and 3rd of February in 2010?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have had the opportunity and, indeed, I used it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And during the course of that interview, did you tell Prosecuting Attorney Mr. Nicholls, and the investigator, Mr. Blaszczyk, the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I told them the truth. There was nothing else that I mentioned but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So do you stand by what you said in that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the transcript that you read, does it fairly and accurately reflect what you said during that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect the gist and the contents of the conversation that was held with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At this stage, Mr. President, Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 29167 which are excerpts from that interview conducted in 2010 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it is common that the witness identifies the relevant document as the one he reviewed, but if there's no dispute between the parties that 65 ter 29167 reflects the statement, then we could proceed. Mr. Stojanovic, I address the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no objection against admission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29167 receives number P2914, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will note that in the 92 ter motion we are also tendering excerpts from the witness's testimony in the Tolimir case. There are some clarifications to be made to that testimony which will be the bulk of my examination today, so what I propose to do is to read a brief summary for the public at this stage and then proceed with my questions, tendering the Tolimir transcript at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence does not object. Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Beginning in mid-November 1993, Colonel Milenko Todorovic was the assistant commander for intelligence and security and the chief of the intelligence and security organ of the East Bosnia Corps. After the fall of Srebrenica, Colonel Todorovic received a task from General Tolimir related to the accommodation of prisoners from Srebrenica at the Batkovic prison camp. Those prisoners never arrived. Colonel Todorovic also gave evidence relating to the command and control of military police units in the VRS structure and the reporting obligations of the corps's security and intelligence organ. That concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, with any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In 1995, Witness, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I held the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly tell us, and I'm not looking for the entirety of the events that happened, but I'd like you just to be as precise as possible in your recollection and tell us what it is that the Main Staff tasked you to do after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Your Honour, the question was what the Main Staff tasked him to do after the fall of Srebrenica. If this has to do with the order which in the summary the Prosecutor said had arrived from Tolimir, the question would have been misformulated. If this has to do with some other order from the General Staff, then a foundation has to be laid before the question is put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, perhaps you ask the witness whether he received any order from the Main Staff in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the question. Did you receive an order from the Main Staff after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I am maintaining now, just as I did in my earlier evidence, with incomplete certainty. I'm not sure if it was given orally or via a telegram. I think -- I'm 90 per cent sure that it was a telegram. It was a short cable from the Main Staff, from the intelligence and security sector. It contained a brief message, conveyed to the corps commander the task whereby accommodation should be readied for between 1.000 and 1.200 prisoners of war who would be transferred to Batkovic in the coming days. As I said, I am 90 per cent sure that these would have been the contents of the telegram. I immediately proceeded to share the contents of the telegram to the corps commander, General Simic, the now late General Simic, who issued orders to other organs to begin preparing the arrangements for the reception of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, now you've told us the number of prisoners that were you told you were to expect to arrive and that they were to be accommodated at Batkovic prison camp. Were you also told from where those prisoners would be coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, this is my recollection, and I can't be sure if it was 1.000 or 1.200 but that was roughly the figure involved. They would come from the enclave of Srebrenica. That was my understanding from the telegram. Previously, news reached us of the fall of Srebrenica. I'm not sure if the telegram said that these were prisoners captured in Srebrenica, but that's probably -- probably what the telegram stated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak closer to the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to come a bit closer to the microphone, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, just so we're all clear, when this order came from the Main Staff from the intelligence and security sector, from whom precisely did this order originate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the order in front of me to be able to give you my comments on it. I assume, and it would have been natural, that the telegram arrived from the intelligence and security department, since I as the chief of the intelligence and security organ of the corps command received telegrams and all other correspondence solely from them. As for the other organs of the Main Staff, they received their correspondence from other organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, I appreciate that you may not remember at this point in time --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But if we can call up 29167, please. And if we look at page 4 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is now P2914, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we look in English at the approximately lines 19, and the B/C/S, it's approximately line 9, you were asked the question: "Q. Okay, are you certain or not certain that the information came from General Tolimir, whether it was in person or by telegram? "A. I am sure about that." Witness, does that refresh your recollection as to whether you were, in fact, tasked by General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This isn't controversial. It's just the issue of whether it was conveyed over the telephone or the telegram that wasn't conclusive. And I did say a moment ago that I am 90 per cent sure that it was conveyed over the -- the telegram and not the -- the telephone within the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And since this order did come from General Tolimir of the Main Staff, can you tell us who he was in relation to you within the command structure?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and assistant commander of the Main Staff. He was assistant to General Mladic, ex officio. According to the intelligence and security professional line, he was my superior. My immediate superior was General Simic as the corps commander. However, in terms of my speciality, which was state security, General Tolimir was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, having received that order, can you tell us were you, at that point in time, eager to receive prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We expected - and I did say this in my earlier testimony - their arrival because within my corps, which is the East Bosnia Corps, there were quite a few prisoners captured, and they were held -- or, rather, there were quite a few members of the corps captured and were held by the BH Army members. As the arrival of these prisoners of war was expected, there was the intention to have them exchanged for our men who would, in that case, be able to reunite with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to the order that you received. Now, you said -- we know from where they were coming, we know the number of prisoners you were to expect. Can you -- you -- you mention very briefly that you were told they would come in the following days. Is -- is -- is that your recollection today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: What I recall of it today is just the task given. I can't recall the exact date when I received it. Was it on the 11th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry -- Colonel, sorry, that wasn't my question. My question is whether in that order that you received you were told when the prisoners would be arriving at Batkovic camp. Was it in a month's time? Was is it in a few days' time? Perhaps I can refresh your recollection, if you need me to.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: From what I remember, no fixed date was given. It was said that preparations should be completed as soon as possible so that we may be ready for receiving them whenever they do come. Perhaps there was a date indicated, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we again call up P2914. If we can take a look at page 3 in the English, page 2 in the B/C/S. And in the English, we can look at approximately lines 3 -- starting at line 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, Witness, you can follow along at approximately line 21. And I'll read the answer you gave: "The point was that we were supposed to prepare the camp so that it could accommodate around 1.200 people who were about to set out the following day."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And then if we go down to lines 14 to 15 in the English. And if we turn a page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we turn the page in the B/C/S and look at the first two lines, you say: "The point was that we were supposed to prepare the hangars for that many people who were about to arrive the following day." So, Colonel, to the best of your recollection, is that, in fact, when you were told the prisoners would be arriving?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was able to read this despite the areas that are blackened out. I can see that here it says "on the following day." But it is not dissonant with what I just said a moment ago, that it should have been done as soon as possible. It implied urgency. Preparations had to be made as soon as possible because they would follow soon after, in a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. But, Colonel, do you stand by what you said that -- do you stand by your recollection of what you said at the time you gave the interview, that they would arrive the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've just said that does not change the gist in any way. On the following day or coming days, in my mind it is quite similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Colonel, now, how was it that you learned about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Officially, it was at the briefing at the corps command that I learned of it. The briefing took place every day at around 1800 hours, if I remember correctly. It was the time when we would learn of all the activities that happened in the area of the corps and beyond, the events of the day, and we would learn of the impending activities for the following day. Before I attended the briefing, I may have heard something about it over the media. However, officially, I learnt of it at the briefing that took place at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, at the corps command meeting, the briefing which takes place at 1800 hours, you would have learnt of what had taken place the preceding 24 hours. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, relative to the fall of Srebrenica, then, do you recall what you told us about when you received the order from General Tolimir at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that I immediately acquainted corps commander, General Simic, with the order that had just come in. He, in turn, issued tasks to the pertinent organs who would implement the order. And that was as far as my duties surrounding the order went.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. But let me go back to my question which was: When relative to the fall of Srebrenica -- so you learn of the fall of Srebrenica at the corps command meeting. How long after that corps command meeting did you receive the order from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Looking back to that time, it's very difficult for me to say if it was 1900 hours, 2000 hours of the day, or in the morning of the following day. At any rate, soon -- there was an order that followed or the order that followed soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So when you refer to 1900 hours or 2000 hours, you're referring to the evening of the corps command meeting when you learned of the fall of Srebrenica? If I can ask you to just put your answer on the record, if you can give your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I meant that day. Actually, it could only have happened at the time the briefing ended and when I went to my office, which was about 100 metres away from the briefing room, and that was when the telegram could have been on my desk. It could have then been 2100 hours, 2200 hours, or perhaps at some point on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you informed General Simic about this order that you received, what did you do in terms of implementation, in terms of implementing that task?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I myself didn't have any direct obligations arising from the order. It was the logistics organs who were supposed to deal with that. Together with the administration in charge of the farm, they were supposed to make sure that the hangar is emptied and readied for the arrival of the men. They were supposed to make sure there was a water supply available, that toilets were ready. It was possible also for me to get involved in these activities at some point down the road. However, these activities were aborted after a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that we -- we -- we all can -- just to remind us, when you say the "activities were aborted," what was it that prompted the abortion of the preparations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As the prisoners from Srebrenica arrived in Batkovic -- or, rather, about the imminent arrival of prisoners from Srebrenica in Batkovic there -- the news spread and very soon families of VRS members who had been captured and were held prisoners were very much expected to see an exchange take place, where these VRS members would reunite with their families. So as the news spread about their arrival, days passed without these prisoners appearing in Batkovic or in the general area. The family members of these soldiers staged a protest and were making inquiries about these prisoners. At Ugljevik, at the headquarters of the 1st Majevica Brigade - most of the members of the captured -- most of the captured VRS members were, in fact, from that particular brigade - there was a crowd that gathered. Quite a few of them also appeared before the corps command. They were asking for answers. They wanted to hear the corps commander tell them what was going on. At this point, General Simic summoned me personally, and this was the order that he gave me, roughly. He addressed me as Toso. That's how he shortened my surname. He told me, Toso, call your boss and find out when the prisoners were coming and what is going on in that department. So I went to my office. I dialled an automatic number and reached General Tolimir directly without going through the switchboard, and I conveyed to him the inquiry by my commander, Simic. This was roughly his answer: You go on and work according to your plan. This task was given up on or was withdrawn. So, in other words, we were supposed to proceed according to our earlier plan because this activity was no longer topical. And this is something that I conveyed to my commander, Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, I'm looking at the clock. Time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Stewart reminds me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you on track as far as time is concerned? You've used close to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's still a few areas still relating to his current testimony I need to cover. I expect to be within the same time but I may be a little bit over depending on the answers I receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same time would bring you already quite beyond the one hour you had scheduled and if we would even go over that --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I don't expect to at this stage, but I have to admit that, depending on some of the answers, it may require a bit more reference back to some of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may suggest to you that you assist the witness in getting closer to your questions rather than to tell the whole background, if you ask what -- how this aborted -- how -- how it was that the task was aborted, then perhaps if you put more detailed, precise questions, then we come closer quicker to the answer the witness finally comes to. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, for your information, you used almost 35 minutes of the 60 you asked for. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Colonel, now, you've told us that this order to prepare Batkovic camp was to be conducted on an urgent basis. Did you go to Batkovic camp, to the hangars, yourself after receiving this order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we can call up 65 ter 30502.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this is the transcript of the interview you gave in 2010.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we turn to page 89 in the English and 78 in the B/C/S. If we look down at the bottom on the English at approximately lines 25, 26, and in the B/C/S it should be around lines 25 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you recall at that time of your interview you pointed out to the investigator that -- on an aerial image that house number 5, the one you had marked number 5, is a house "that I personally visited when we heard that around 1.000 to 1.200 prisoners were supposed to arrive and because it needed to be emptied so that they could be accommodated there ..." And you go on. Does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not you visited the hangars at Batkovic camp once you learned of the order?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When I said no, I had in mind the period between the reception of the order and the moment when I conveyed it to General Simic. Later on, as the order was supposed to be implemented, at some point in time, I did visit the location to see if the preparations were developing as planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, it is your evidence that the military police activities do fall within your sphere of responsibility as assistant commander for intelligence and security and that you -- that there were approximately 20 military policemen who worked in shifts of about ten, guarding Batkovic camp. And you've also stated, given evidence, that that number of military policemen was not sufficient to secure a thousand to 1.200 prisoners. So my question for you, Colonel, is did you have the opportunity to discuss or propose to your corps commander the -- the engagement of additional military policemen before you received the instructions to cease preparations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud. And we'll be strict on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not discuss it with General Simic. As the preparations developed, it was understood that they should include all those who were supposed to be engaged in them. From the logistical point of view, what was needed had to be prepared to have them accommodated, and the camp warden was tasked with requesting additional resources, personnel, catering personnel, guardsmen, et cetera. It was dealt with during the process of preparation. Given the fact that the preparations ceased, we never got to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But, Colonel, it was, wasn't it, within your responsibility to make a proposal to the corps commander about additional military policemen. Could military policemen be engaged without your proposal to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In principle, I was supposed to make that proposal. But in urgent situations or when things are developing quickly, the camp warden could request a reinforcement of 20 to 30 soldiers. But we never actually got to that point because all activity was halted in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Colonel, you've -- you've told us that you had daily briefings with the corps commander and other staff. Before the instruction came to cease preparations, was there an opportunity at any corps command meeting for you to make that proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There were opportunities at every meeting, if I was requested to do so. I don't remember whether that request was made and whether I did put forth proposals because we are discussing a very short interval before activities ceased. What I can remember, in terms of implementing that task, was that I went to see for myself how far these physical preparations went. I saw a -- a loader and a truck and grain was being -- and wheat was being put on the truck in preparation of their arrival. This is a detail I still have in mind. But as for the rest, it would be difficult for me to recall them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, if we could take a look at 65 ter 30492. And at page 27, you had been asked there about the engagement of a contingent that was required for securing the expected prisoners. And you say at lines -- if we look at -- it would be around lines 2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, that should be transcript page 12952. So it's ... we have to turn two more pages. 29. We are at 12953. It should be the previous page, 12952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any chance that there's an incomplete upload, Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That could be possible, Your Honour. I don't think so, but I can resolve the issue by turning to -- if you just give me a moment. If we turn to -- I think we can pick it up on Sanction, T12952.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, I can start reading out what it is that you said. So this is in relation to the engagement of additional military police, and you said: "It did not happen solely because further preparations were stopped for their reception." Do you stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by what I said, as I have said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, the page you referred to is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I think we're just trying to pull it up in Sanction for everyone to see. I have quoted the relevant part. Okay. There we go. At lines 2 -- beginning at line 2: "It did not happen solely because further preparations were stopped for their reception."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you previously told us that it was your responsibility, in fact, to propose to the corps commander the engagement of these military policemen and then you subsequently said that you were waiting for a request. A request from whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Lukic, I address you. Next time if Mr. Mladic talks at this volume again, we'll not accept it. It's just whispering, inaudible for anyone else in this courtroom. Mr. Mladic, it's up to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following this short discussion, I'm afraid I no longer remember your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I can repeat it. Previously you told us that it was your responsibility, in fact, to propose to the corps commander the engagement of these military policemen and then you subsequently said that you were awaiting a request. From whom did you expect a request to come in from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As per regulation, it was the camp warden who could launch such request, based on the opinion of the commander who was in place with the 20 military policemen. In consultation, they could decide that they were short of men and then he could request of me, through the commander, to provide additional military policemen for security. In that case, I would have proposed to the commander to add an additional number of military policemen as estimated. It did not materialise because the task was dropped.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, given that -- given that the -- you expected this request from the -- the camp warden and since you were told that these prisoners were going to arrive the following day, would you not expect the camp warden to have already put in that request very, very early on, perhaps ...?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I probably did expect it. The camp warden and the others were engaged in the physical preparations first and foremost. This would have been a simple thing, to take ten minutes and bring, say, another 20 MPs from the barracks to the collection centre. It would have been an easy and simple task to deal with, as compared to the other tasks that were supposed to be part of the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the mounting pressure from the families who were eagerly awaiting the prisoners to arrive so that they could exchange their soldiers. And I'll just refer the Chamber to P2914, page 3, lines 31 in the English, page 4, lines 20 in the B/C/S, where you describe that pressure. And, in fact, you state that this pressure mounted within 24 hours of having received the order. And my question to you is: Given the pressure on the command, your corps commander and yourself, did you, shortly after there was, as you describe it, a mutiny of sorts at the corps command, follow up on these families' requests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There was no mutiny at the corps command. No pressure was placed on me personally, and I did not take part in any conversation with those family members. It wasn't up to me to clarify it for them. It was done by the corps commander, General Simic. He summoned me and asked me to verify what was going on with the prisoners and how far things advanced.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, it was -- I was, in fact, using your words from the Tolimir case where you say there was almost a mutiny of sorts. But moving on from that, do you stand by your evidence that you gave in the interview, P2914, that it was quite soon after the families surrounded the corps command that your commander, General Simic, instructed you to contact your boss, General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it. The explanation provided should be taken in a relative sense. But I do stand by the -- the gist of the argument. I had received the task as specified, and I contacted those I was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you recall the evidence that you gave in the Tolimir case, and General Tolimir, during his cross-examination of you, asked you about the evidence you gave to the Prosecution during their questioning of you, during the direct examination by Mr. Vanderpuye. And in -- in the course of that cross-examination, and we can call this up. It's -- in Sanction at T13138, lines 4 to 12, and I'll read out what you were asked by General Tolimir: "Q. When providing this interview" - and that's a reference to the 2010 interview in Belgrade - "did you always repeatedly say that you were uncertain about the time precisely because a lot of time had elapsed and that you cannot be specific as to the date? "A. Yes. "Q. Is there a possibility that later on, when questions were put to you and insistence placed on confirming something you cannot recall, you made certain changes to the original interview you provided in Belgrade? "A. Partially, yes. But the gist of my original statement remains unchanged." Do you stand by the testimony you gave?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do -- can you confirm that your recollection of these events was better at the time you gave the interview in 2010 than your recollection in 2011 during the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Relatively speaking. It is a relative question, as a matter of fact. Perhaps I gave it some thought afterwards, and then I presume I could recall a few details, although there are very few that I can recall after so many years. However, I still maintain that the gist of it -- well, whether it was one day or two days, from this point in time it is very difficult for me to decide and to stand firmly by saying one thing or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, moving on to your testimony in the Tolimir case --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No one put any pressure on me in the sense that I should opt for this or that date. Perhaps it was my reasoning. I was searching for the most logical answer as to how things may have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So that's -- sorry. Colonel, that's what you did in the Tolimir case. But was your recollection at the interview -- you stand by your recollection that -- the evidence you gave then?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So just in relation, then, to the testimony you gave in Tolimir, and this is your testimony between the 18th and 21 April 2011, can you tell the Chamber whether you recently had the opportunity to listen to the evidence you gave in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I listened to my evidence in court, and I read the first statement I gave in Belgrade on the 2nd and 3rd February.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, with the clarifications and the evidence that you've given today, does your Tolimir evidence, the evidence you gave in the Tolimir case, the -- the -- what -- that you heard, does that fairly and accurately reflect what you had told the Trial Chamber in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 30492, which are excerpts from the transcript of this witness's testimony in the Tolimir case.

utterances.text: Defence has no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.text: Your Honours, what remains is the admission of the exhibits associated exhibited to that testimony. And if I may, I'll just read those out. 65 ter 4138.

utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, two issues: The first one, adding it to the 65 ter list; second one, admission.
