utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is hereby on the record. P01515 is in evidence already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Todorovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go briefly through the internal structure of the organs and services you were a part of as of November 1993 in East Bosnia Corps. You will agree with me that there was only one intelligence and security organ in East Bosnia Corps throughout the time without having ever been divided into two organs.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You assumed the duty of the intelligence and security organ in the East Bosnia Corps in November 1993, taking over from your predecessor, Petar Jovanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Petar -- but his name was not Jovanovic. His name was Jakovljevic. Both of them have died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, there was a commission for the exchange of prisoners of war in East Bosnia Corps, was there not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The commission was headed by Ljubomir Mitrovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of hierarchy, was the commission subordinate -- subordinated to your intelligence and security organ?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, it was subordinated to the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of the establishment, was Ljubomir Mitrovic assigned to the intelligence and security organ within the staff?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Formally he was on the list of members of the intelligence and security department. As he was appointed to be the head of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, he was released from all duties in the intelligence and security organ and was solely concerned with the duties covered by his position as the chairman of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, or the president of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the defence area of the East Bosnia Corps, was there a -- the Batkovic camp that was active under their purview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And within whose jurisdiction did the Batkovic centre come?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The Batkovic collection centre had its commander, who was corps commander's immediate subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards and the security detail assigned to the Batkovic collection centre, were they members of the military police of the military police battalion of the East Bosnia Corps, or were they completely independent of the system?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They were members of the 3rd Battalion of the military police of the East Bosnia Corps resubordinated or attached to the collection centre. They were held answerable for their day-to-day work to the camp warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties and obligations as the chief of intelligence and security organ and assistant commander for intelligence and security in respect of the Batkovic collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Just as was the case with all the other organisational units of the corps command, where it came to the collection of intelligence about what was possibly unlawful activity, where it came to the prevention of such activities, providing support to the superior officer on security issues, where it came to the use of the police, there was nothing special to it. It was the same sort of duties that I had to discharge in respect of those organisational units that did not have their own intelligence and security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If there was news of crimes being committed in the Batkovic collection centre, if there was news of someone overstepping their authority, whose duty would it have been to investigate into the matter and possibly have it prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Upon receiving such information, it was my duty and obligation to, first of all, brief the commander on the specific issue and to take measures that were within my authority, to engage members of my service to collect information, to engage the elements of the military police who were tasked with pre-charge investigations with the recovery of trace evidence of the alleged crime, and, if it had to do with a crime, I was also duty-bound to inform the investigating judge. There was a military court that was active in the town of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As of November 1993 through to the end of the war, had you ever been informed to the effect that there were reasons to suspect that a crime had been committed in the Batkovic collection centre against the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I had never received this sort of information either officially or inofficially. There may have been information to the effect that somebody was slapped about, something like that, but I did not have any knowledge of any violations of human rights having been committed there, and that's why I didn't take any steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point, inform the Main Staff of the VRS about the possible abuse or, as you called it, slaps that were meted out in the Batkovic collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned slapping about, I didn't mean that I had information to that effect. I just took it as an example. I didn't have this sort of information or any other information. And, therefore, there was no need for me to inform my superior along the professional line in the Main Staff. There were health problems, but the doctors in the health centre in Bijeljina addressed those. There was even an inmate of the camp who died. It was established that his death was of natural causes, though, resulting from something else. This information was shared with the representatives of the Red Cross who had their office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the representatives of the ICRC have, as of November 1993, open and free access to the Batkovic collection centre?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Our work was open, transparent, and proper. Even the office of the president of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and the secretary there kept -- was always kept open to everyone. Everyone was free from that office to come and visit the Batkovic collection centre, and they would come often with items of personal hygiene, tracksuits, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In what way were the prisoners of the Batkovic collection centre provided with food and meals after November 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is something I said in the earlier trial as well. To my knowledge, this -- the -- the food that we were served from the kitchen facility in Bijeljina, that same food was served to the Batkovic collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the medical treatment of these prisoners. Can you tell us who was the physician tasked with providing medical care to these prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I can state under responsibility that the medical centre in Bijeljina was tasked with that duty. And even when he was not called, there was a physician who would come once or twice a week. I don't recall the name of the person, but I recall that we did choose -- or, rather, the physician chosen was of Muslim ethnicity to make it easier on the prisoners. And he would go there and choose the right treatment for these prisoners. That I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many prisoners of war were there, in the awareness that the number did fluctuate, between November 1993 and the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There was a group of about 20 of them from the Cazin Krajina. They were refused entry anywhere, but they managed to leave to third countries. They were permanent residents, if I can even call them, of that centre. As for the rest, there were between 20 and then 50. However, after the fall of Srebrenica, sometime around the 20th - and this is an approximation - between the 18th and the 20-something, 20-something, there were around 171 of them. And I did refresh my recollection the last time I was testifying about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P2922. If I noted down the number correctly, this is the document that was just admitted. It's an aerial image of the Batkovic facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since there are markings there already, can you try and remember what was the facility where prisoners were present up until July 1995? If you can, based on the markings that you made?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Before July 1995, they were put up in the facility number 2. Yes. The facility north-west of it was the one where preparations were under way for the reception of prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, if you can remember, what the size was of the facility that is marked by number 2 in this image?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'll give you a number which may be correct and may not be. At least 10 by 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we continue, north-west makes, for the Chamber, only sense if we know what the orientation of the photograph is. Otherwise, north-west could be in any direction. Could you assist us? Perhaps we could ask the witness to say which construction he referred to when he referred to what was north-west of number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the number shown on the photograph of the facility you had in mind when you said that it was in the north-western part.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: These are my numbers, but they're not very nice, though. It is the facility number 1. The reception is number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your assistance. Let me ask you something about the commission for exchange. We heard evidence about the exchange of non-Serb population who left Bijeljina and the process was organised by a Mr. Djurkovic as the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the East Bosnia Corps. If you know this person, I would like to ask you whether he had any connection with the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I know him. I had an opportunity to meet him. He had nothing to do whatsoever with the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska. Through certain officers, he tried to establish some kind of contact or whatnot, but it was the corps commander's order, and it was my position as well, to keep him as far as possible from our tasks and obligations. The -- there was the official exchange commission which was in operation. They had all the necessary records, and it was a sound organisation. Now, what he did and on whose behalf, given the situation with the civilian authorities, the civilian police and the military authorities, he did not fall under any kind of responsibility or scope of the military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that any potential exchange of POWs organised and conducted by the Army of Republika Srpska went through the exchange commission which was headed by Mr. Ljubomir Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was several such exchanges, and they were all provided under the competence and with the knowledge of the ICRC. Any prisoner which went to either of the sides received a certificate from the ICRC, in terms of his or her date of capture and exchange. It was all in keeping with the conventions which regulate such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of defence of the East Bosnia Corps there was another facility which you mentioned - not today during direct examination but in your previous testimony - called Vanekov Mlin. Please tell the Court what kind of facility it was and under whose authority was it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The facility itself and its name, Vanekov Mlin, well, it is to be found immediately next to the Bijeljina barracks, just across the street from the entrance to the barracks. It used to be a mill owned by a certain Vanek. As a building it is quite run down. However, in the courtyard, there was space used by the military police battalion. They kept their vehicles and other assets there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it -- sorry I sorry to interrupted you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival, rather early on, maybe in early January 1994, upon my proposal to relieve the military police battalion of some unnecessary tasks, the command -- corps commander decided and established a garrison command. In addition to other elements, there was also a military detention facility which was placed in -- on the premises of Vanekov Mlin. The military garrison detention facility was secured by military policemen who were somewhat older or of poorer health. A squad was dedicated to that task coming from the military police structure of the East Bosnia Corps. They were resubordinated to the garrison commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Petar Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll stop just in time for a break. But before that, I wanted to ask you whether the person in question is Jovanovic or Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I assumed my duty from Jakovljevic who then went to Banja Luka. Petar Jovanovic remained. He is from Modrane [phoen], a nearby village. He remained in Bijeljina. He was a retired lieutenant-colonel, and even after the war he remained at the post of garrison commander. I'm quite certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We will resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I briefly address the Defence. The Chamber was, in a similar way as the Defence, unpleasantly surprised by the new court schedule because we were not consulted on it, and there's a fair chance that a solution will be found. So, therefore, instead of asking for an urgent response, the Chamber, at this moment, is exploring the responsibility of resolving the matter. But we were not amused either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be that I have missed something in this respect. If that's the case, I perhaps should have chosen different words, but let's proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, thank you for your understanding concerning the need we put forth regarding Mr. Mladic's health.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, briefly I'd like us to go through a particular rule and then to deal with issues of command and control and documents covering that area. It has to do with your potential conversation with General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter 04375 in e-court. Page 1, please. And then could we have page 7 in e-court in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, these are the rules of service of security organs in the armed forces. Before moving on to specific paragraphs, let me ask you this: Was this the basic document in terms of your work during the war in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the starting or basic document concerning our work. It contains a number of rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree that, through your education and training, you had occasion to rely on the rules of service as one of the basic documents concerning your work?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at page 7 then in both versions because I will seek your assistance in a matter. Have a look, Colonel. We have the tasks of security organs before us. It is specified what security organs do. Please look at items (d) and (e), and then I will put a question. In item 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, (d).

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version it would be on -- actually, I would like to go to the next page because I'm interested in paragraph 7, item (d). Can we also go on the next page in English as well, which would be page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 7(d), we see that security organs perform specialist administration services for military police units. Please assist us. What would that mean, in a practical sense? Were you able to issue orders to the military police of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In item (d) you quoted, it states professional supervision or specialist administration services of military police units. It is a different concept from command. Commanding is issuing specific orders on the use of resources and implementation of tasks. Specialist management means control, supervision, providing particular equipment, conducting training on specific topics, and so on and so forth. So command is something a commander does; whereas specialist management is done by his assistants within their respective scopes of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us put that in a practical situation. Say there's a need to engage a part of the MP battalion of East Bosnia Corps in the area of defence of the Drina Corps. Who is the person who, in this specific case, can issue an order to the MP battalion commander of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The exclusive right and duty to carry out such engagement by issuing an order lies with the corps commander or his assistant or another person standing in if he is currently absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, then, to say that if we stick by 7(d), as part of the system, it would be the corps commander who would have the right and obligation to ask you as a professional organ of the command whether that would be necessary, proper, and what assets and weaponry would need to be provided to that part of the MP battalion from the East Bosnia Corps when performing tasks in the area of another corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The corps commander, as well as any other level of command, is independent in making his decisions in terms of use of his subordinate units. He is under no obligation. It would be ridiculous if he would ask a subordinate whether he could do something. Under normal conditions, when there's discussion of initial engagement of all units including the military police, his assistants, including myself, can propose the best use of resources. The assistant commander for artillery would do that for his scope. I would be in charge of the military police, and so on and so forth. In exceptional situations, there is no need or possibility to consult anyone. The commander is authoritative, and he decides on what units or part of units would be engaged in performing a specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you specifically: Do you recall one thing which you mentioned in your previous interview, as well as in the redacted part, which is not part of the evidence in this case, do you recall being consulted at any point in time by General Novica Simic, commander of the corps, on the use of part of the MP battalion in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do not think so. Unless it concerns the situation where my commander, General Simic, ordered to convey something to the MP battalion commander, Major Vulin. It was for him to assign and equip a reinforced squad with the necessary vehicles which were to be sent to the Zvornik Brigade to assist in reception and transport of POWs to Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about that, Colonel, and we will go through a number of documents. But let me first explain why I asked you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have P1513 in e-court. It is an order -- actually, it was an interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at the document once it is on the screen. Please focus on paragraph 2 of the document. The then-Zvornik Brigade commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, informed the Drina Corps Command -- Colonel, do bear in mind that this is the 16th of July, 1995, probably sometime in the morning since telegrams were sent in the afternoon from the Zvornik Brigade. In any case, in item 2, we see the following: "Our forces," and then he specified a MUP company of 100 men, two platoons from the Bratunac Infantry Brigade. And now the part I wanted you to focus on: "Part of the military police platoon from the IBK," which is East Bosnia Corps, and then the document goes on, "are carrying out decisive defence in the brigade zone, sealing off and searching the terrain in the wider area of Planinci, Crni Vrh and Kamenica." My question is this: Do you have any knowledge about parts of the MP battalion from the East Bosnia Corps on the 16th of July sent to the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In my testimony, I kept insisting on the fact that I didn't have any knowledge about this and that this did not happen, in fact. However, at the end of my testimony, I was shown the operative diary or log-book of the corps duty officer which read that upon the order from the Main Staff, that deputy corps commander, so deputy to Simic, ordered the commander of the MP battalion, Major Vulin, to send overnight to the area of Zvornik Brigade some 50 MPs in order to carry out certain military duties. Except for me seeing that document - and I have no reason to do doubt it - I know nothing of this. It goes to prove the point that we were looking at a moment ago, item 7 of the rules of service, that the corps commander or his deputy or anybody else standing in for him will have the full right to order the engagement of an entire unit or elements of it - in this case, an MP battalion - without consulting anyone on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is precisely what I'm asking you about. Would it be fair to say that the command and control system and the system of single authority imply that such orders would go up -- down the chain of command: Main Staff, corps, and the corps' subordinate units, and -- and definitely not through the security organ's line?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If that is the case, can you explain the following to the Trial Chamber. I understand that you will not be aware of the date. However, at one point, as you say, you received an order, a report, an instruction. Can you tell us what exactly it was that you received from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any material, in physical terms, and I did speak about it in Belgrade and during my testimony. So I don't have it on a piece of paper. Now, the information that I received down the chain of command of the speciality organs, whether it was that I should convey the information to my superior that preparations should commence, and try as I might, I cannot recall what the form of the information was, but the gist of the information was that Tolimir - that's to say, the intelligence and security sector - tasked me with conveying specific information to my corps commander, which had to do with preparations for the reception of prisoners, and I did as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now -- now my next question. In view of the rules of service and your earlier answer, would you agree with me that if things happened this way, then it did not happen according to the process of control -- of command and control and -- and the superior/subordinate relationship, as defined in the army by law?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Literally speaking, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this conversation or the -- during -- or -- or in that document, was it ever mentioned to you any possible involvement in this of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I can claim with full certainty that General Mladic's name was not mentioned. However, as an officer who has some understanding of the chain of command, I can only conclude the following. In terms of the lawfulness of the document or the information that I received, had someone - the name doesn't matter - had anyone from the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff been in the vicinity of the chain of command and had they been told, Convey the information down your chain to the corps commander for these preparations to take place, so it would have been a round-about way, but it would still have been within the bounds of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, if I may briefly consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may consult. But he is strictly ordered to keep the volume of his voice so that no one can hear it, apart from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour? May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 65 ter document 30502 in e-court. It's a -- or, rather, it's the unredacted version which was admitted into evidence as P2914. Let look at page 35 in English and page 32 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, P2914 is 65 ter 29167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'll ask you to focus on the portion that I need to you look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we skip three pages forward in the B/C/S version, please. Three pages forward, please. The next page, please, in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please look at line 23. This is where the investigators put the following question to you: "We have the information that on the 12th of July, 1995, General Tolimir came and had a meeting with you and with" -- and we're missing the rest. And you're answering: "The security command -- the security department." And then the investigator says: "Yes, the security department of the East Bosnia Corps." Then you go on to say: "I cannot be sure about the dates but I will tell you what I was tasked with in relation to that. If this happened as a result of a direct contact with him or by telegram, it is very difficult for me to be certain after so much time." And then you go on to say: "To convey -- I was supposed to convey to the commander, basically support the idea that -- so that around 1.000," and then you say again 1.200 people captured in Srebrenica could be brought there and be put up in Batkovic. So I'm asking you this: If the system of command and control is operational as is the superior/subordinate relationship, would it have been in keeping with the rules of service to go through assistant commanders for security and intelligence of the Main Staff of the VRS to go down to their security organs in the East Bosnia Corps for them to get in touch with their commander, or would it have been proper instead to go down the chain of command itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It would have been properly done had it gone down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this interview, the investigator, Tomasz Blaszczyk, told you: We have information that General Tolimir did arrive and met with you. Were you at any point given any sort of information or proof that on that day, the 12th or any other day, General Tolimir was in direct contact with you at the East Bosnia Corps? Were you provided with any proof of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This was not the case. I -- I could not recall this during this interview on the 2nd and 3rd of February and I was convinced that there was no physical meeting. I thought about it later on, and I still maintain today that we did not meet in person, that this took the form of a written document. In other words, I did not meet with General Tolimir either in the area of responsibility of the East Bosnia Corps or in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You do know that it is a historical fact that, to this day, no physical trace has -- has been found of this telegram. There is no indication of it ever having arrived.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to where this telegram, if it had arrived, could be found? Where it would be physically located today?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: As the war ended in Bosnia-Herzegovina and before I left the duty that I had until that point and joined the Army of Yugoslavia, I remember a document arriving, an order from the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff of the VRS that a list should be drawn up of all the documents that had been sent to the security organ of the East Bosnia Corps and all the other units. It was an order that was sent to all the security organs in the Army of Republika Srpska. This list was to be drawn up, an inventory made, and this was to be submitted to the Main Staff for their further use and storage. This order was fully implemented. The documents that were kept in the intelligence and security organ of the East Bosnia Corps were all included there, but I cannot tell you where they are at present. I -- I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not customary, since most of the officers of the VRS of the professional soldiers, trained soldiers, was it not customary for all of them to have had diaries, to have kept diaries where they would have detailed their daily activities? Didn't you yourself have such a diary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I did not keep a diary of my own activities. I had a notebook where I would make note of the more important meetings and the subjects discussed. There were several such notebooks, and as I was leaving my service for the VRS, I destroyed the contents of all these notebooks because they -- they did not have the validity of a document. All the documents that I had, I handed -- handed them over to the appropriate service with the staff, the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I consult with the client for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Briefly, and at low volume. We'll be very strict on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if this conversation took place over the radio, do you recall how it was set up, that radio communication at your end, and where exactly, from what location did that call from the chief of intelligence and security department of the Main Staff come? Do you know where he was physically located at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: When I was inquiring about the prisoners and why they were not coming? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we're still dealing with that initial, first conversation, where you were asked to tell your commander that between 1.000 and 1.200 prisoners would be coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I said that I was 90 per cent sure that it was a telegram. So I allow for the possibility that the information was communicated to me over the telephone but that's just the 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go with the 90 per cent. So where would that telegram have arrived from? What was the code of the sender?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's really hard for me to say without looking at the telegram. General Tolimir may have been at Pale, and then the telegram that would have been drafted in that unit closest to his location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know, tell us; but apparently you do not know, tell us as well. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Or perhaps the witness -- apparently when he said, when asking for clarification of the question, whether you're asking about him inquiring about the prisoners and why they were not coming -- do you know how you got in touch and where Mr. Tolimir was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please try to respond. Although it is completely acceptable if you don't know. Just say so.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. Can you tell us where you were when the telegram arrived? Who handed it to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was in my office. It was physically brought to me by the organ which was from the corps command. It had -- it contained their code as well as signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a result of any kind of legitimate fighting, that there is a possibility of POWs being captured?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It would have been quite logical that if there had been POWs, they would have been accommodated in an appropriate facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And for the collection centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous question was useless. The present question is about logic. It -- really, we don't need a witness to explain to us that if you take a large amount of prisoners of war, that you have to leave them somewhere. That is really -- if someone doesn't understand that, then I would not expect him to be on this Bench. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would the area of the collection centre at Batkovic meet the conditions necessary to have POWs accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is -- Mr. Mladic should not speak aloud. Not to anyone. Mr. Stojanovic, this question, it's -- it's -- it's all about -- you want to make the message about prisoners of war. That's fine. The Chamber understands the position of the Defence in that respect. But in view of what the witness told us before, he considered this to be a place where you could accommodate a larger number of people. That's why he talked about logistics, et cetera, et cetera, so there's no need to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Let me conclude the topic with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As part of the information you received, as well as the request as to what was to be conveyed to your corps commander, did you see in it anything that would be unlawful?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about dates. You say that you cannot remember the point in time when this memorandum or a telegram or a phone conversation or even General Tolimir appearing on the premises of East Bosnia Corps -- well, let me try and ask you to recall at least whether it was in the morning or in the afternoon. Was it night-time? Day-time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I definitely cannot tell you the date with any certainty. As for the time of day, whether it was night-time, day-time, well, I can be a bit more certain about that. Speaking from this point in time, I seem to remember having found General Simic in his office, so during the working hours. So it may have been in the morning or afternoon. He showed me -- I showed him the document and he read it. This is what I seem to recall, in terms of procedure. Now, whether it was at 8.00 a.m. or 2.00 p.m., I can't say from this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any idea what time elapsed until when you received another task from your commander, General Simic, to call General Tolimir to check what was going on with the arrival of POWs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be completely precise on that point either. But I am positive that more than one day must have passed but also not more than three to four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do try and tell us this: In your view - and you have already discussed it in the redacted portion of your interview - where did you find General Tolimir when you called him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I remember the following. When I called him to obtain information about when they would be arriving and what was going on with the POWs, I called a direct number from my office, and he picked up the phone. So I called his number in his office. Early on in the conversation I mentioned some number, and then the real figure of 165 came to my mind, which I recalled in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to determine it more closely. After your conversation on the phone with General Tolimir, when was it that General Simic called Vinko Pandurevic, inquiring with him whether he had any POWs in the area of responsibility of his brigade? How much later did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Shortly afterwards. I went from my office to General Simic's office where I told him that there was nothing doing, that things were stopped. He called Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic. Perhaps an hour or two later, he called me again and tasked me with -- well, I don't know whether it was one, two, or five hours, so take it conditionally speaking. But he tasked me with conveying his order to the MP battalion commander to implement what we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is my reasoning correct then, that on the day when you had the telephone conversation with General Tolimir, is the same day when the part of the MP battalion from East Bosnia Corps left for Zvornik in order to take over the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That would be the most logical conclusion. Perhaps if it was in the afternoon, a decision was made for prisoner security not to have them transported during the night but to bring them in the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at any point in time in the course of those few days you received POWs from another area and brought them to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In terms of my knowledge and engagement ... let me repeat. In terms of my knowledge, and in terms of engaging any MPs from the East Bosnia Corps, no such things happened that I know of. Perhaps there was a unit from the East Bosnia Corps or some other unit which brought one, two, or several prisoners to Batkovic because there were such examples in the previous period. But I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'd like to take the witness back to a previous matter. I asked you earlier, Mr. Todorovic, I asked you whether -- when you were inquiring about the prisoners and why they were not coming, I asked you: "Do you know how you got in touch and where Mr. Tolimir was at that time?" Then Mr. Stojanovic intervened and said: "Please try to respond although it is completely acceptable if you don't know. Just say so." Your answer was: "I don't know." Five minutes later, Mr. Stojanovic asked you: Tell us, and you've already discussed it, where did you find General Tolimir when you called him? That was at the same occasion seeking information -- or is that a different one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it is my question which caused the confusion. It actually referred to another conversation the witness had with General Tolimir a few days later, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I hope that it has been clear to the witness -- Mr. Mladic, one second, please. One second. Please be seated. You will have an opportunity to consult. I would first like to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said you can later consult, not now. One second, please. I consult with my colleagues. You wait for a while, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You then answered that question when put to you by

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "I remember the following. When I called him to obtain information about when they would be arriving and what was going on with the prisoners of war, I called a direct number from my office, and he picked up the phone. So I called his number in his office." That apparently was a telephone conversation when you were not yet aware that the whole thing had been cancelled. Now, one second -- if you say -- you -- apparently you are gesturing that I may make a mistake. Please explain yourself on this to be a different -- or at least to be a telephone conversation where you were aware already that it was cancelled. Please explain yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief. My first response, when I said that I don't know where General Tolimir was, had to do with the initial information, the initial tasking I received to carry out preparations to accept the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then -- I stop you immediately and then I read exactly to you what happened. You were asked: "Do you know where he was physically located at that point?" And then you answered, you said: "When I was inquiring about the prisoners and why they were not coming? Is that what you mean?" Then Mr. Stojanovic said: "No, no, we are dealing with the initial ... conversation where you were told by your commander that ..." And then your answer considered. Then at the end of this matter, you said you did not know where he was when you received these initial instructions. You said he may have been in Pale. And then the telegram would have been drafted, that unit closest to his location. And then I said to you: If you know, tell us, but if you don't know, tell us that as well. Apparently you did not know where he was during the initial instructions. Then I said: "Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic." And then I said: Or perhaps the witness, when he -- I think said when he asked for clarification of the question, whether you're asking him inquiring about the prisoners and why they were not coming, do you know how you got in touch and where Mr. Tolimir was at that time? That is, when inquiring about why they were not coming. Then Mr. Stojanovic intervened and said it would be completely acceptable if you wouldn't know. And then you said: "I don't know." I asked you, the first time, clearly about the moment when you were inquiring why -- where the prisoners of war were and -- not coming. When asked the same question by Mr. Stojanovic, you gave a detailed answer. I just wanted to put this clearly on the record. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since I'm about to call up a document, perhaps this would be the right time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the right time for a break. The witness can be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us where we are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that I still have half an hour left, and I will be within the time given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is expected to remain seated. I don't have to repeat -- first seated before consultation. Mr. Lukic, we're not playing games. Okay. Mr. Stojanovic, you were answering my question. You said half an hour left. Yes. Then, Ms. Hasan, there is a small chance you might need more than three or five minutes. Could you give us an estimate? As matters stand now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: As matters stand now, I would estimate 15 to 20 minutes. But I'm -- I'll reassess that during the break and see, indeed, if we can let the witness go at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if everyone would be very disciplined and very brief, we might be able to finish. If not, we'll have to do the last part tomorrow morning. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we stopped when we were discussing the point at which the East Bosnia Corps commander was contacting the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and giving you instructions about the deployment of elements of the MP battalion. Let's look at P2918 together. P2918. I think that you were shown this document while you were being proofed by the Prosecution. It's a list of persons to be transferred under guard issued by the 5th MP Battalion of the East Bosnia Corps -- the 3rd Battalion of the East Bosnia Corps military police. So the persons were escorted on the 18th of July, 1995, at 1600 hours, and they ended up at Batkovic. Now this group of 22 individuals, does it correspond with what you recall were, indeed, the individuals who were transferred to and admitted into Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That's what the list says. It's a general document. It doesn't bear the signature of the person who would have received these individuals on the 18th of July at 1600 hours. Let's assume that this is what happened. During my earlier testimony, I saw these same individuals among the -- among the individuals who were, indeed, admitted into Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In P2137 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2317"], there is a list of Muslims who were exchanged from the Batkovic collection centre. All of the 22 individuals listed here were exchanged, and this was with the involvement of the 2nd BH Army Corps. It says here at the top of this document: Military post code 7118 in Han Pijesak. And it also reads: The 5th Battalion of the military police in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion. Mr. Stojanovic, two corrections. I think you said P2137, not 2317. And this document is labelled 3rd Battalion not 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. With all due respect the heading reads: The 5th Battalion of the military police in Vlasenica. Supposedly someone who would have been the author of the document. That's what my question was about, if I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you be more specific about what the -- this involved? Who is it that the 3rd MP Battalion of East Bosnia Corps would be taking this group of 22 prisoners from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You've presented the situation as it transpires from this document. The 3rd Battalion would be taking charge of these individuals. However, what is missing at the bottom of the document is the place where this hand-over took place, time, date, and signature. So anything I would say at this point about any of these things would be just speculation, and I don't want to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the indisputable fact that we agreed upon, which is that these individuals were admitted into Batkovic and subsequently exchanged, would this date, the 18th of July, correspond to that point where your corps commander, Novica Simic, told you to convey information to the MP battalion that they should go ahead and take charge of the prisoners who would be exchanged on the following day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I can see here and based on my earlier knowledge of that broader list, I think that the day when they -- the first prisoners arrived in Batkovic was the 18th. So these would have been the first prisoners to arrive there. And I think that it was in the afternoon on the 17th that I conveyed this information to the MP battalion commander, and that then he proceed to implement the task on the 18th to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and that was the first contingent of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am trying to, in fact, reconstruct the chronology of the events. Would it be fair to say, then, that the conversation that you had with General Tolimir over the phone could have taken place on the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we're not exploring possibilities. We're exploring facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I am asking the witness to testify to the facts. And since the witness was not really precise in terms of when the conversation took place, I will try to explore this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness could tell us, then he is invited to do so. But to put four, five different portions of evidence to him and say whether it is likely or unlikely that this would have been the day is something that is argumentative, and if you put that evidence together, you can raise such an argument before the Chamber. The witness is supposed to tell us what he knows, and you should focus on that rather than to ask him whether it could have taken place on the 17th of July. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, having seen this document, and having confirmed to me that you established that the first group of prisoners arrived in Batkovic on the 18th of July, does this here refresh your memory as to when that conversation between you and Mr. Tolimir took place? And I mean the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The dates here and the arguments from today and before do point to such a conclusion, although I do not remember that it was -- or whether it could have been the 17th, the 18th. It could have been day or two before this date at least ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will not press the matter anymore. I would like to focus your attention on something else now. In the East Bosnia Corps, did you have information about the intensity of the fighting on the 16th of July in the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade and the breakthrough of the 28th Division column in the direction of the BH Army-held positions.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we did. Though this was not relevant to what I was doing, so I don't remember the details of what happened in which part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, let's look at the 65 ter document 07463. 07463. Colonel, during proofing for your testimony you were shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll have several questions about it, about its format, in fact. Do you remember that this document, in fact, is a summary of the conversation that you had on the 6th of May, 1995 in the East Bosnia Corps Command with the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic, and Momcilo Krajisnik, as well as Major-General Bogdan Subotic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I remember the talks. I was present there. In my earlier testimony before this Tribunal, I was shown a report drafted by General Simic which I wasn't aware existed, although I did attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were one of the participants in the meeting, do you recall, in fact, that this followed the Assembly session in Sanski Most, the Republika Srpska Assembly session, and that it followed an open conflict between the political and military leadership which took place?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The very subject matter of the discussions points to this fact, so there's no reason to believe otherwise. Though the issues discussed in Sanski Most was not something we were aware of. We knew that it had to do with certain removals from posts in the army but nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While it is beyond dispute that Colonel General Ratko Mladic, on 26th of April, 1995, following the Republika Srpska Assembly session in Sanski Most, came to the East Bosnia Corps and informed you of the events that transpired during that Assembly session. My question to you is: Did you attend this meeting with General Mladic on the 26th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I was probably -- most probably was. I can't remember. I can't remember possibly where I was on the 26th or -- 19 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should refrain from any comment by gesture or by words. Otherwise ... smiling, nothing. Please proceed, but I'll only do so, Mr. Stojanovic, after I've drawn your attention to the fact that when you earlier said that the witness had established that the first group of prisoners arrived on the 18th, I read to you what the witness really said. He said: "Based on what I can see here and based on my earlier knowledge of that broader list, I think that the first prisoners arrived Batkovic was the 18th." He has not established anything. He has drawn conclusions from a document and from portions of his memory. Please refrain from misrepresenting what the witness said. And you may now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is my question: Do you recall at all the report that was drafted and distributed to each and every soldier of the East Bosnia Corps on the current military and political situation authored by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It seems to be coming back to me now. I seem to remember that this report did reach us and was sent to all the units with a request that all the personnel be acquainted with the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if, at any point in time, any senior or commanding officer of the East Bosnia Corps was called upon to in any way resist or stand up to the political leadership or to engage in any sort of activities that would be akin to a coup d'état?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. I had information to that effect and I am convinced that the relationship between the army structure and the political structure nationally and locally was unburdened by any problems and free of any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Stojanovic please repeat his reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're invited to repeat the reference you apparently requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Page 3 in B/C/S, page 6 in English, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of he document which is still on our screen, I take it, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. For the transcript, it is 07463.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this report by General Simic, we find the following. After President Karadzic, Major-General Novica Simic, the IBK commander, addressed the meeting. He first greeted the guests on behalf of the IBK command. General Simic noted that, in principle, it was not right for the Supreme Commander to criticise a superior officer before lower-ranking officers who are subordinated to him. He added that the report in question was a truthful rendering of General Mladic's briefing and had not been fabricated in the corps. He especially emphasised that there had never been any coup orientations within this corps and, had there been any, he would have certainly prevented them and reported to the Supreme Command. He repeated his request that the problems that have arisen be resolved at the necessary level in such a way as not to undermine the efficiency of our defence forces. Do you recall whether at that moment President Karadzic as the supreme commander mentioned any ambitions on the part of the military leadership to execute a coup d'état?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall the details of that conversation. I don't remember things turning unpleasant during the consideration. Now whether President Karadzic told this to General Simic without the presence of assistant commanders, maybe then he said that it wasn't right for the supreme commander to criticise his superior in his presence. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the same document, can we look at the last paragraph of page 5 in the B/C/S version and the last paragraph on page 10 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "During the discussion, President Karadzic said that General Gvero wrote General Mladic's speech for the Assembly which is why he bears responsibility for the problems which arose. General Gvero came to his own Supreme Command in the company of eight men in bullet-proof jackets, which is a disgrace for a general. There have been rumours that somebody wants to kill General Mladic, which is absolute nonsense and a lie. When General Mladic was undergoing a crisis, we were under the impression that he deliberately rushed in front of the front line in order to be killed, and we issued an order for his protection to prevent him from being hurt." Colonel, given the fact that you were present at the meeting, were you at any moment under the impression, bearing in mind the information provided by General Mladic ten days before the meeting, that he had any kind of ambition to carry out a putsch and assume power in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I have never had that impression, including the time in question. Quite the contrary. He was modest and carried out his duties strict -- in a strictly military fashion. He did not get involved in politics without allowing any local-level politicians to interfere in military affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Bearing in mind that you were there, and so as not to go even deeper in the topic, but you are aware of the discussion by Colonel Jelacic, Slobodan, who was assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, he stood by all that was contained in the report provided by General Mladic. Having all that in mind, was it your view that the situation in the VRS was precisely as General Mladic had put it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your service with the VRS between November 1993 and until the end of the war, did you ever receive any kind of direct or indirect knowledge that General Mladic was in any way involved in the difficult, ugly, and tragic events concerning Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Until the present day, I have never obtained any kind of knowledge of that kind, including the time of my service. Later on, after I retired, I no longer researched or inquired about the matter, since it was out of my hands. I didn't inquire about General Mladic or anyone else in terms of those who were assigned responsibility for the atrocities which took place in Srebrenica. It was outside the area of the corps where I served, and I simply didn't need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this may be a good time to tender 65 ter 07463 in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I have no objections, except to correct the record which at transcript page 66, line 19, may have correctly or incorrectly, I don't know, recorded Mr. Stojanovic as saying that this document was used during the proofing of this witness. And it was not -- at least not for this testimony, for today's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- at least it's not evidence from the witness but it was an assumption, I took it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07463 receives number D438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, exactly the author of the document is who? You said is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our information, which we received from this witness, and according to what was stated in the 2nd of February interview, and as was mentioned in the proofing, the author of it was Novica Simic, commander of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that appear anywhere from the document itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It was not signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the witness also told us that nothing was said about a coup or whatever. Is it the position of the Defence that this is a false report of what happened during that meeting? Or what is it? I have some difficulties in understanding exactly what it is used for because the witness said nothing was said about the coup, nothing unpleasant. However, I have not read the whole of the document, but if you read some parts of it, then I wouldn't be pleased if I would be criticised in this way. What's the -- what's the position of the Defence on this document? Does it accurately reflect what happened during the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our belief that it accurately reflects what took place at the meeting held at the corps command on 6th May 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, at the same time, the witness, in many respects contradicts what happened there, where he said, I think, he was present. Now, which of the two? Is it the testimony of the witness which we have to rely on or on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was present and in his interview of 2 February he said that, according to his recollection, this document accurately reflects most of what he can remember of the meeting. The sentence quoted as having been ascribed to Novica Simic was that he informed the supreme commander that in this corps, there had never been any kind of coup orientations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- having said this, I'd like to thank the witness and we have no further questions of him. I was told by the Prosecution that there will be no need for re-direct. Thus I may have overstepped my time-limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's first -- I got the impression that the Prosecution did not fully agree with that. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: There must have been some misunderstanding. There is it some re-direct to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time do you assess would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Reasonably I would say I should be done within 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's the first thing to do tomorrow morning. Mr. Todorovic, we adjourn for the day. We need still some time tomorrow to conclude your testimony. Before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given today or still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.30, in this same courtroom, III. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I'd like to put clearly on the record that when I earlier today said that the Chamber was unpleasantly surprised by the new schedule and that we were not consulted on it, and that we were not amused, that the Registry is not in any way to be blamed for that but it's, rather, internal communication, perhaps within the Chamber. So, therefore, this should not be misunderstood. We, nevertheless, will try to resolve the issue in relation to which I made these observations. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 26th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.
